newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Arthuis sees pension funds in place in 97.
newsitem.headline: France's Arthuis sees pension funds in place in 97.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Thursday he had high hopes private pension funds would be available to French people from next year onwards.

He was speaking during a parliamentary debate likely to lead to approval on Friday of a bill on retirement savings schemes which has languished for two years, hit by French hesitation about opening up to Anglo-Saxon style pension funds.

Arthuis confirmed the funds, which will be set up through a joint agreement between employers and employees, will be allowed to pay out 20 percent of pension money in a lump sum, while the rest will be in annuities.
The compromise ended a fierce debate which pitted banks, favouring lump-sum payouts, against insurers who wanted payouts in annuities.
He also said that employee contributions to pension funds would be exemmpt from income tax up to a limit of five percent of gross salary.
Employer contributions would be exempt from social security contributions up to a limit of 4,000 francs a year or two percent of annual salary.
Those ceilings appear to be the result of government fine-tuning at the last minute to ensure it is not accused of favouring private pension funds over the existing system.
It has long insisted that the new funds will complement rather than replace the current system of universal pensions.
The parliament was thought likely to vote in favour of the bill on Friday, parliamentarians said ahead of the debate.
"I have high hopes that these retirement savings funds will be available to our citizens from next year," Arthuis said.

The funds will be managed by insurers, banks or mutual groups. The government is likely to stipulate the funds can invest a maximum of around 60 percent of their assets in bonds, sources involved in talks on the funds have said.
Unlike Britain and the United States, where pension funds are huge stock market players, France depends on a system where the cost of paying pensioners is levied from the wages of today's workforce.
It has spent years discussing how such funds should be set up, running at times into accusations from unions of privatising the welfare system.
The opposition Socialist party on Wednesday slammed the government's pension funds plans, calling them "a new step in the attack against the welfare system."

The government has said pension funds will channel badly needed money into France's undercapitalised companies and breathe life into the stock exchange, which is tiny compared to those in London and New York.
